content.title: Difference Between Observational Studies and Experiments
content.overview: On the SAT Math exam, distinguishing between observational studies and experiments is key to evaluating statistical claims. The core difference lies in whether the researcher actively intervenes with the subjects, which directly determines whether the conclusion can only reveal a correlation or can infer causation.
learning_objectives: Identify the defining characteristics of observational studies and experiments
Distinguish between active intervention and passive observation
Determine the type of conclusion (correlation vs. causation) supported by a specific research design

sections.title: Observational Studies
sections.content: An observational study is one in which the researcher collects data and observes relationships between variables without intervening with the subjects. The researcher simply records what has already happened or is currently happening. For example, surveying whether people who exercise frequently have better sleep quality than those who do not. In this case, the researcher did not force anyone to exercise; they only observed natural behavior. Because uncontrolled external factors exist, observational studies can only conclude that there is a "correlation," not prove "causation."

sections.title: Experiments
sections.content: An experiment is a study in which the researcher actively applies a treatment or intervention to the subjects to observe its effect on the outcome. The key feature of an experiment is "intervention." To establish causation, experiments usually randomly assign participants to an experimental group (receiving the treatment) and a control group (receiving no treatment or a placebo). If the experiment is rigorously designed (especially including random assignment), the researcher can conclude "causation"—that the treatment caused the change in the outcome.

sections.title: Core Comparison: Intervention and Conclusion
sections.content:
The fastest way to distinguish the two is to ask: Did the researcher change the participants' behavior? If yes, it is an experiment; if they only recorded it, it is an observational study. The strength of the conclusion varies accordingly: observational studies support "A is associated with B," while experiments support "A caused B."

![Research Design and Conclusion Logic Flow](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/3d31ccb1-30f8-4714-86d7-0fef8bb9c167-1786502084382-834.webp)

worked_examples.question: A researcher wants to know if drinking green tea lowers blood pressure. He selects 100 volunteers and records their usual green tea intake and blood pressure levels. He finds that people who consume more green tea generally have lower blood pressure. What type of study is this, and what conclusion can be drawn?
worked_examples.solution:
1. Identify characteristics: The researcher did not ask the volunteers to drink green tea; he only recorded their existing habits. This is "passive observation."
2. Classification: This is an observational study.
3. Conclusion: One can only conclude that "there is a correlation between drinking green tea and low blood pressure." It cannot be said that drinking green tea caused the reduction in blood pressure because other factors (such as dietary habits) might influence the results.

worked_examples.question: A researcher randomly divides 200 volunteers into two groups. The first group drinks three cups of green tea daily, and the second group drinks an equal amount of water. After three months, the average blood pressure of the first group is significantly lower than that of the second group. What type of study is this, and what conclusion can be drawn?
worked_examples.solution:
1. Identify characteristics: The researcher actively assigned the treatment of "drinking green tea." This is "active intervention."
2. Classification: This is an experiment.
3. Conclusion: Because there was random assignment and intervention, a causal conclusion that "drinking green tea caused the reduction in blood pressure" can be drawn.

common_mistakes: Mistakenly believing that observational studies can prove causation: This is the most common trap option on the SAT.
Confusing random sampling with random assignment: Observational studies can have random sampling, but only experiments have random assignment (treatment allocation).
Ignoring the "intervention" criterion: Assuming that any data collection is an experiment, when in fact a treatment must be applied.
exam_tips: Look for words like "assigned," "treated," or "controlled" in the problem; these usually point to an experiment.
If the question asks for the "most reasonable conclusion" and the study is observational, avoid options containing "caused" or "because of."
Conclusions for observational studies typically use softer language like "associated with" or "linked to."
content.recap: Observational studies discover correlations by recording data in natural states; experiments prove causation by actively applying interventions and random assignment. On the SAT, only well-designed experiments can support causal claims.

knowledge_claims.content: An observational study is one in which the researcher collects data without applying any intervention.
An experiment is a study in which the researcher actively applies a treatment or intervention to subjects to observe results.
The key to distinguishing an observational study from an experiment is the presence of "active intervention" on the subjects.
The results of an observational study can only indicate that a correlation exists between variables.
A well-designed experiment (including random assignment) can support a conclusion of causation.
It is incorrect to draw a causal conclusion from an observational study because uncontrolled confounding variables may exist.
In an experiment, researchers typically divide participants into an experimental group (receiving treatment) and a control group.
Unlike experiments, researchers in observational studies only record pre-existing behaviors or characteristics.
If a study describes participants being "randomly assigned to different groups," it is usually an experiment.
If a study only surveys people's eating habits and measures weight, it cannot prove that a certain food caused weight change.

items.stem: Researchers recruit 80 participants, randomly assign them to two levels of sleep duration, and compare an outcome. What type of study is this?
items.explanation: B is correct. The researchers impose treatments and randomly assign participants.

items.stem: Researchers record the naturally occurring study method of 85 participants and compare it with an outcome without assigning any treatment. What type of study is this?
items.explanation: C is correct. The researchers observe existing conditions without imposing a treatment.
